title: Moved instead of stopped
roles: Sent abusers away and received them
summary: When a priest, brother, teacher or headmistress was found abusing children, the institution often moved them rather than calling the police: to another parish, another school, another state, or another continent. The map draws 26 documented moves recorded by inquiries, courts and the institutions' own files, and colors every country that sent or received an abuser. The Pennsylvania grand jury found bishops moved abusers between parishes; Bishop Mulkearns knew of Gerald Ridsdale's offending by late 1975 and kept reappointing him to new parishes; the Adass Israel School paid for Malka Leifer's 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel before police were told; the Makin review called John Smyth "a problem solved and exported to Africa".

facts.t: Pennsylvania grand jury — six dioceses: A 23-member statewide grand jury report released by Attorney General Josh Shapiro on 14 August 2018 identified 301 'predator priests' and at least 1,000 child victims over about 70 years in six dioceses. The roughly 1,400-page report found bishops 'went to great lengths to keep it secret' and moved abusers. Most crimes were too old to prosecute.

Diocese of Ballarat — Gerald Ridsdale and Royal Commission Case Study 28: Ridsdale moved through about 13 postings 1962–1991; Mulkearns knew by late 1975; a senior police officer in 1972 offered a detective promotion to stop investigating Monsignor John Day

Malka Leifer — Adass Israel School, Melbourne: In March 2008, after a teacher confronted her, the school arranged and paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for Leifer and four of her children without telling police. In Israel, then deputy health minister Yaakov Litzman pressured ministry staff to alter psychiatric evaluations so she would appear unfit for extradition; her lawyers sought more than 70 hearings and appeals.

John Smyth — Iwerne camps, Zimbabwe and South Africa (Makin Review): A 1982 internal Iwerne Trust report (the Ruston Report) described the beatings; the Makin Review found an 'active cover-up' by its recipients; police were not told until 2013. The review called Smyth 'a problem solved and exported to Africa' and found no evidence of proactive attempts to alert Zimbabwean authorities.
Diocese of Stockton — Fr Oliver O'Grady: Bishop Mahony ordered him away from one family in 1980, then moved him to a new parish in 1984 before a psychiatric evaluation was complete

University of Zurich pilot study (Dommann and Meier), commissioned by Swiss Bishops' Conference, RKZ and KOVOS; report May/Sept 2023: 1,002 cases, 510 accused, 921 victims; superiors systematically transferred accused clerics, sometimes abroad, to avoid prosecution

uncertain: The moves drawn are only those a source documents; most church and school personnel files were never opened, and Poland's state commission reported in 2022 that files sent to the Vatican were out of its reach. A move is drawn from where the abuser was sent from to where they went; whether the receiving diocese or country was told is often not recorded.
implications:
Moving an abuser protected the institution twice: it avoided a police report at home, and it put the abuser among children who had no warning. The receiving places were often poorer or more remote (Africa, the Pacific, Latin America, Indigenous communities in the Canadian north), where victims were less likely to be believed and courts less likely to reach a foreign priest.

For a reader, the point is that the pattern was not a few bad decisions. The same move appears in Catholic dioceses, Anglican and evangelical circles, an ultra-Orthodox school and a Scottish private school, decades apart and on four continents. When an institution is allowed to handle abuse internally, relocation is the cheapest option it has, and it is the one these records show it chose.

title: Years of waiting: protected by status
summary: For 42 cases the sources date both the first complaint that reached police, a church, an employer or officials, and the first conviction, charge or official finding. The middle wait is 12.5 years. A pupil told police about the MP Cyril Smith in 1968 and was told Smith was "a very important, powerful man"; in 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged and had been assured in 1970 that he would not be. Complaints about Jimmy Savile reached police from 1958; investigations in his lifetime brought no charges. Athletes complained about Larry Nassar from 1997. Each country is colored by the longest wait among its cases.

Colonia Dignidad (Paul Schäfer) (Chile): Escapees' allegations in the 1960s (Wolfgang Müller; Heinz Kuhn 1967) were rejected by politicians because of the colony's ties to those preparing the 1973 coup; colony served as a DINA torture centre

Mount Cashel Orphanage (Canada): Royal Newfoundland Constabulary probe opened Dec 1975 was closed by the police chief nine days later; the Justice Department ordered the report rewritten (1976); Deputy Minister of Justice said further action unwarranted (1977)

Malka Leifer (Adass Israel School) (Australia): The school flew her to Israel in March 2008 before police were told; Israeli Deputy Health Minister Yaakov Litzman interfered with psychiatric assessments, later pleading guilty to breach of trust; extradition took six years from her 2014 arrest
Johnny Kitagawa (Japan): Shūkan Bunshun's 1999 series; Kitagawa won a defamation judgment (2002) but courts upheld the abuse reporting (2003-04); Japanese mainstream media barely covered it

uncertain: The first-report year is the earliest complaint a source documents; earlier complaints that left no record are not counted, so most waits are longer than shown. Two people included were acquitted (George Pell, Bishop Franco Mulakkal); their rows record the time to charge, not a finding of guilt.
implications:
A long gap between the first complaint and the first action is the clearest sign of protection, because it shows that someone knew. The mechanisms in these records repeat: a lenient deal (Epstein's 2007 non-prosecution agreement), a police chief closing an inquiry nine days after it opened (Mount Cashel, 1975), complaints passed over because of who the accused was (Cyril Smith), witnesses attacked or killed (Asaram Bapu, Timothy Omotoso), and media that would not repeat a court-upheld story (Johnny Kitagawa in Japan, 1999–2023).

In several cases action came only after the accused died. For a general reader, the lesson is that the age of a case is not evidence it was unknown. When a famous or powerful person is finally charged, the useful question is who had the complaint before, and what they did with it.

title: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
roles: Lobbying against reform and bankruptcy filings
summary: Most survivors disclose decades later, after the legal deadline to sue or prosecute has passed. Where legislatures tried to lift those deadlines, the institutions facing claims lobbied against it, and when the deadlines fell, many filed for bankruptcy. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018; in Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Catholic Conference spent over $7.6 million and the insurance federation nearly $20.7 million from 2014 to 2024. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and orders filed for bankruptcy, several within hours or days of a trial, a deposition or a new law.

uncertain: Lobbying totals are what these organisations spent on all issues in each state, not only on limitation reform; the disclosures do not split them. A bankruptcy filing is legal and does not itself prove an intent to avoid victims; the timing and the asset transfers are what the records show. Outside the United States, lobbying against reform was not documented in the sources reached.
implications:
Abuse cases are decided as much by calendars and accounts as by evidence. A deadline that runs out at 21 or 23 ends most cases before survivors are able to speak, so the fight over that deadline is a fight over whether the cases exist at all. The records show the institutions with the most claims spending to keep the deadlines, and insurers spending even more.

When the deadlines fell anyway, bankruptcy capped what survivors could recover and stopped trials that would have put files and bishops on the record. The Milwaukee archdiocese moved $57 million into a cemetery trust in 2007 with the Vatican's approval, writing that it wanted protection from legal claims. For a reader, this is where "behind the scenes" is literal: the outcome is set in committee rooms and bankruptcy courts, long before a survivor reaches a judge.

title: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
summary: Official inquiries into institutional child abuse came in waves: Canada and Ireland first (Hughes, 1989; the Ryan commission, 1999–2009), the United States in 2002–2004, most of western Europe after 2010, Australia's Royal Commission 2013–2017, then France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland from 2021. Where inquiries used population surveys, the numbers were far above church records: about 216,000 minors abused by French clergy and religious since 1950, against about 3,000 identified before. Many "national" studies were commissioned by the church itself. Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, with some of the largest Catholic populations, have no national inquiry in the sources reached.

title: States that shielded their own
summary: When the accused belongs to another state, a diplomatic service or an army, prosecution depends on that state. UN peacekeepers fall under their own country's courts: at least 134 Sri Lankan soldiers were accused of abusing nine Haitian children in 2004–2007 and none was convicted. The Holy See recalled its nuncio to the Dominican Republic, Józef Wesołowski, and told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow his extradition. South Korea's court refused to send the Welcome to Video operator to the United States. Morocco's king pardoned a Spanish child rapist as a gesture to Spain. Israel's deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments that kept Malka Leifer from extradition for years.

The Holy See has said it acts through its own tribunal; its refusal to share files with the Irish and English inquiries is documented, its reasons are its own.
implications:
Immunity, extradition rules and military jurisdiction were built to protect diplomats and soldiers from hostile governments. In these cases they protected people accused of abusing children, and the children were nearly always in the poorer country: Haiti, the Central African Republic, the Dominican Republic, Morocco.

The pattern runs through respectable institutions, not rogue ones: the UN, the Holy See, a democratic court in Seoul, Israel's government. For a reader, the practical point is that "the matter was referred to the home country" usually means it ended there. The rare exceptions, such as France's request that led the Holy See to lift a nuncio's immunity in 2019, came when the victims' country was powerful enough to insist.

title: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
roles: Sending country, later closed or suspended
summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad from 1953 to 2008; its Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that the state was responsible for human rights violations in those adoptions. Romania (1990s), Guatemala (until 2007–08), Cambodia and Vietnam, Nepal, Ethiopia (banned 2018) and others followed, each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or registered as orphans. Receiving countries then began to look at themselves: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after the Joustra committee, and China ended it in 2024. The map colors each sending country by whether it was later closed or suspended and draws 59 documented flows.

facts.t: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents.

Guatemala — notary-run adoption trade to the US (1996–2007): After the civil war ended in 1996, adoptions abroad rose each year, run almost entirely (about 98%) by private notaries who handled both sides without court review and charged $35,000 or more per child; 97% of children went to the US. CICIG's 2010 report studied 153 cases and found 78% violated the new law in some way.

Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights.

Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank.

China — Hunan orphanages bought trafficked babies for adoption (2005 convictions): Six Hunan orphanages were found buying infants from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong, placing nearly 1,000 children with domestic and foreign families between 2002 and 2005. In 2005, according to Xinhua, 23 civil officials were fired; three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years and six others to 3–13 years.

uncertain: Totals are adoptions reported by 23–25 receiving states (Peter Selman's tables) and miss countries that do not report; South Korea's total differs by source (163,898 per its ministry for 1953–2008; up to about 200,000 in AP reporting). A closure means the sending or receiving government stopped or suspended adoptions; the reason given was not always fraud.
implications:
Demand for babies sat in a few wealthy countries (the United States, Spain, France, Italy, the Netherlands, the Nordic states). Supply came from wherever paperwork was weakest and poverty deepest, and the fees paid per child made the paperwork worth faking. Each time one country was exposed and closed, agencies opened programmes in another; the timeline shows the closures following each other across continents for half a century.

The records also show who knew. South Korea's commission found the state itself responsible; the Dutch government admitted in 2021 that its officials had known of wrongdoing for years and failed to intervene. For a general reader, this means a legal adoption and a trafficked child could be the same child: the court order was real, the "orphan" status was not, and the receiving country's approval laundered the rest.

facts.t: Argentina — junta's 'systematic plan' to appropriate babies (2012 verdict): On 5 July 2012 Federal Oral Criminal Tribunal No. 6 of Buenos Aires found that the military junta had run a systematic plan to abduct children born to detained or disappeared mothers, between 1976 and 1983. Former dictator Jorge Videla was sentenced to 50 years and the last dictator, Reynaldo Bignone, to 15 years; nine other defendants received 15 to 40 years (MercoPress).

Russia — deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children; ICC warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova: On 17 March 2023 ICC Pre-Trial Chamber II issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova for the war crimes of unlawful deportation and unlawful transfer of children from occupied Ukraine to Russia, committed from at least 24 February 2022.

Indian Residential Schools — Truth and Reconciliation Commission and abuse claims: About 150,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit children attended federally funded, church-run residential schools; the last closed in 1997. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission's final report (December 2015) documented 3,200 deaths and said the true number is much higher.

Denmark — 1951 'little Danes' experiment: 22 Greenlandic children removed: In May 1951 Danish authorities, with the Red Cross and Save the Children, sent 22 Greenlandic Inuit children to Danish foster families to re-educate them as 'little Danes'; they were supposed to be orphans but only six were. Six were adopted in Denmark and 16 returned to a Danish-speaking orphanage in Greenland and never lived with their families again.

Spain — children of Republican prisoners taken by the Franco regime: A 1940 law allowed imprisoned mothers to keep children only until age three, after which the state took custody; 12,043 Republican children were in state custody in 1943. In 2008 Judge Baltasar Garzón characterised the removals as crimes against humanity and said the Falange was involved in kidnapping or forcibly repatriating children and changing their names.

uncertain: Numbers of children removed are estimates in most of these cases, and several differ by source (Ukraine's government counted 20,651 children deported or forcibly displaced; Russia disputes the framing). Spain's courts have not convicted anyone for the stolen babies; the one doctor tried (2018) was acquitted on the statute of limitations.
implications:
These removals were not hidden crimes by outsiders; they were carried out by ministries, courts, churches under government contract and armies, with paperwork. The children taken were nearly always from the group the state was trying to suppress or absorb: political prisoners, Indigenous peoples, colonised islands, unmarried mothers, an occupied country.

This is the clearest case on the map of abuse and trafficking run from the top. For a reader, the pattern explains why denial lasted decades: the officials who would have investigated belonged to the same state, and recognition came only after a change of government (Argentina after 1983) or a later generation's inquiry and apology (Australia's apology in 2008, Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission in 2015, the Netherlands in 2021, South Korea in 2025).

title: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
roles: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
summary: Child sex tourism followed enforcement around the map. When Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, Svay Pak in Cambodia grew; when Cambodian police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid was announced in advance and nearly all the children were moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. When Manila closed Ermita in 1992, businesses moved to Angeles City. Offenders' home countries passed laws to prosecute their citizens for abuse abroad (Germany 1993, Australia 1994, Canada 1997, Japan 1999, the US PROTECT Act 2003). Then the trade moved online: in the Philippines, street and establishment child sex trafficking fell 79–86% in targeted cities (2006–2016), while monthly Philippine internet addresses used for child sexual exploitation rose more than twelvefold (2014–2017).

summary: Children in war zones and camps were abused by the people sent to protect or feed them. A 2002 UNHCR and Save the Children report documented aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food for sex with children. In Haiti, more than 100 Sri Lankan peacekeepers were sent home in 2007 over the abuse of children; none was convicted at home. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014–2016. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators in the WHO-led Ebola response in Congo (2018–2020), 21 of them WHO staff, with victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly allegation counts since 2004.

MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent — child sexual exploitation ring, Haiti: In November 2007, 114 members of the 950-strong Sri Lankan contingent were accused of sexual misconduct and abuse, and 108, including three officers, were sent home.

Ebola response, North Kivu & Ituri — Independent Commission on SEA by WHO and other responders: The Independent Commission appointed by WHO reported on 28 September 2021 that it identified 83 alleged perpetrators, 21 of whom were established with certainty as WHO employees during the response; most were Congolese staff hired temporarily who used their authority to obtain sex, often in exchange for jobs.

uncertain: The 2016 per-country troop figures were extracted automatically from a UN annex and have not been checked against the printed table. French judges dismissed the Sangaris case in January 2018, so it is shown as alleged.
implications:
Crisis zones combine the conditions abusers need: children who are hungry and alone, outsiders who control food and safety, and legal immunity. The UN cannot prosecute troops; only their home governments can, and the records show those governments rarely did. Allegations fall and rise with each new mission rather than declining steadily.

For a reader, the pattern explains why "peacekeepers accused" headlines recur every few years without convictions. The system is designed around sending soldiers home, not putting them on trial, so the main sanction available is repatriation. Change, where it came, came from leaks and whistleblowers (Bosnia 2001, the Central African Republic 2015), not from the reporting system.

Armed groups abduct and sell children because it pays twice: it rewards fighters and it terrorises communities into submission. Courts have caught up with a few commanders (Ongwen, Ntaganda) years later, but most of the children taken in Iraq, Nigeria, Uganda and Sudan were never recovered or counted.

For a reader, the pattern shows that the largest trafficking of children in recent decades did not need secret networks; it happened in the open, in front of the UN, and was documented as it happened. What was missing was not knowledge but the power or will to stop it.

summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect child-abuse networks are common. The records sort them into what was proven, what was disproved and what is still only claimed. Proven: Chile's secret police (DINA) used Colonia Dignidad, whose leader was convicted of abusing 25 children, as a detention and torture site, and Germany admitted its embassy looked away. West Berlin's youth authorities placed boys with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, from the late 1960s, on a psychologist's advice. US troops in Afghanistan were told not to intervene when allied commanders abused boys. UN police monitors and US contractors in Bosnia bought trafficked girls. The FBI and Australian police ran abuse sites for weeks to months to identify users. Disproved: the Kincora inquiry found no evidence MI5 used the home for blackmail; the Met's Operation Midland "VIP ring" was invented by a man later jailed for it. Claimed, not established: that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency.

facts.t: Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site: In 1966 a teenager who fled took refuge at the West German embassy; the embassy sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. German diplomats praised it as a 'model colony'. Federal President Gauck said in July 2016 that German diplomats had for years looked away; Foreign Minister Steinmeier in April 2016 shortened the closure period of Foreign Office files from 30 to 20 years to release them.

Afghanistan — bacha bazi by Afghan forces; US troops told not to intervene; SIGAR 2017: NYT (2015) reported US soldiers were instructed not to intervene, in some cases even on US bases; US law (Leahy) required cutting aid to offending units but SIGAR/NYT reported that never happened. Capt. Dan Quinn was relieved and Sgt 1st Class Charles Martland initially separated after beating an ALP commander who admitted chaining and raping a 12-year-old boy (2011).

Playpen / Operation Pacifier — FBI ran the site for 13 days: After seizing the server the FBI kept Playpen running from 19 February to 4 March 2015 under a court warrant and used malware (a 'Network Investigative Technique') to unmask users; the EFF criticised the operation as continued distribution, and the 11th Circuit (2019) held the warrant invalid but did not exclude the evidence (good-faith exception).

Kincora Boys' Home (Belfast) — claims of MI5/army intelligence complicity: Abuse allegations reached the RUC by 1977 without prosecution until 1980; the Hart inquiry found a 'catalogue of failures' by police and authorities. Former army officers Colin Wallace and Brian Gemmell said in 2014 that superiors stopped them passing on or pursuing information.

Claims that Epstein was tied to intelligence services: In July 2019 journalist Vicky Ward (Daily Beast) cited an anonymous former White House official saying Acosta told transition vetters he had been told Epstein 'belonged to intelligence' and to leave it alone. Acosta denied this, and DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility (Nov 2020) found no evidence Epstein was a cooperating witness or intelligence asset.

implications:
The documented record is less cinematic than the rumours and in some ways worse. States did not need secret rings: a dictatorship used a cult's compound because it was useful, an allied army's abuse of boys was tolerated because the alliance mattered more, a city youth office placed children with known paedophiles for decades, and police chose to keep abuse sites running for weeks to catch more users.

For a reader, the pattern is a way to sort claims. Ask what an inquiry, a court or the agency's own files established. Where that exists, the role of the state was real and named. Where only an anonymous source or a single witness supports it, it stays a claim, and spreading it can damage real cases, as Operation Midland did for survivors whose allegations were later doubted.

implications:
Every step of online abuse passes through a company that could see it: the server host, the app, the payment processor, the bank. The records show these firms acting mainly after outside pressure (a sheriff's letters to Visa and Mastercard over Backpage, a newspaper column over Pornhub, a regulator's case against Westpac), and design choices such as encryption that cut the reports police depend on.

For a reader, the money and the hosting are where this is most traceable. A child in Pampanga, a viewer in Melbourne and a server in Sofia are linked by transactions that pass through regulated companies. Whether those companies look is a policy choice made in boardrooms and legislatures far from any of the three.

facts.t: Global: Childlight 2026 meta-analysis covers 103 data sources, 147 studies and only 60 countries with representative survey data on technology-facilitated CSEA (studies 2006-2024)
South Asia: Lacking in representative survey data (Childlight 2026); only 2 countries / 2 sources for past-year online solicitation (6.5%, low confidence)
West & Central Africa: Lacking in representative survey data; a single study for past-year online solicitation — no pooled estimate possible
Middle East & North Africa: Lacking in representative survey data; not represented at all for online solicitation; one source for unwanted sexual content
Online sexual exploitation (all regions): Past-year sex-disaggregated estimates rest on only four studies in three regions; lifetime estimates on three data sources
Sexual extortion (all regions): Sex-disaggregated estimates based on only 5 studies

Global (2024 index): Childlight Dec 2024: one in eight (12.6%) of the world's children — about 302 million — experienced non-consensual taking, sharing or exposure to sexual images/video in the past year; 12.5% (300 million) online solicitation. The 2026 update did not produce a new single overall estimate because no new studies measured overall prevalence

Global (2026 update): Pooled estimates: online solicitation 26.6% lifetime / 6.7% past year; CSAM/IBSA 5.2% / 1.6%; unwanted sexual content 8.7% / 7.3%; online sexual exploitation 9.6% / 2.4%; sexual extortion 9.1% / 2.5%
Global (2026, Nature Human Behaviour): 1 in 5 women and 1 in 6 men experienced sexual violence as children; more than 130 million children in 2024; from 1,412 studies in 147 countries

uncertain: The regional groupings follow UNICEF's regions, which Childlight uses; individual countries within a region may have national studies that were not pooled. "No national inquiry found" for Brazil, the Philippines and India is an absence in the sources reached, not a sourced statement.
implications:
An empty space on a map of abuse is easy to read as safety. The records show it usually means the opposite: no surveys, no inquiries, few reports to international systems, and in many places the same institutions that would be investigated controlling the files.

That is why this map estimates where nothing is documented, using the size of the trafficking trade, modern slavery, online reports and how little stands in the way, and marks those countries as estimates. For a reader, the honest statement about most of Africa, South Asia and the Middle East is not that children there are safer, but that the world has chosen not to count, and that the estimates suggest the problem is at least as large as where it has been counted.

title: False alarms that drown real cases
summary: Invented trafficking stories take resources from real ones. In July 2020 the US National Human Trafficking Hotline received hundreds of reports about a false claim that the furniture seller Wayfair was selling children; the hotline's operator, Polaris, said the volume made it harder to help people who needed it, and none of the reports had new information. "Pizzagate" led to a man firing a rifle inside a Washington restaurant in 2016. London's Metropolitan Police spent over £2 million on Operation Midland, built on a "VIP ring" story invented by Carl Beech, who was himself jailed for child-abuse offences. The McMartin preschool trials in the 1980s cost about $15 million and ended without a conviction.

uncertain: Operation Underground Railroad and the "Sound of Freedom" story are contested; this map records only what investigations established. A claim being unproven does not make it false; it means no court or inquiry has established it.
implications:
False stories about secret elite rings do two kinds of harm. They pull police time and hotline capacity away from children in real danger, and they make the next real allegation against a powerful person easier to dismiss as one more conspiracy theory. The Midland collapse was used for years to question survivors of real abuse in Westminster and elsewhere.

For a reader, the protection is the same test this map uses throughout: what did a court, an inquiry or a primary record establish? The real cases on this map, including those involving princes, prime ministers' friends and bishops, were proven through that route, slowly. Viral claims skip it, and the children they claim to protect gain nothing from them.
